lesson.title: Collecting the Numbers: What Is a Data Set
lesson.summary: A data set is an organized collection of values, called data points, gathered by counting, measuring, or observing something, and it is the raw material used to look for patterns and relationships.
lesson.body:
A data set is a group of individual values collected about something, such as a list of quiz scores, the heights of every student in a class, or the daily high temperature recorded over a month. Each individual value inside a data set is called a data point, or sometimes an observation. A data set can be small, like five quiz scores, or enormous, like millions of temperature readings, but it is always simply a collection of the numbers, or categories, gathered for one purpose.

Data comes in different types. Numerical, or quantitative, data consists of actual numbers that can be measured or counted, such as test scores, heights, or temperatures. Categorical, or qualitative, data consists of labels or categories rather than numbers, such as a favorite subject or an eye color. Both types of data can be organized into data sets, though numerical data sets are the kind most often plotted and compared using the coordinate plane tools covered in upcoming chapters.

Here is a simple worked example. Five students take a quiz, and their scores form the data set 85, 90, 78, 92, 88. This data set contains 5 data points. Even without any formal statistics yet, you can look at this organized set as a whole: the smallest value is 78, the largest value is 92, and every number in between tells you something about how that group of students performed. Listing the numbers in order, from 78 up to 92, already makes the data set easier to read and compare than a random, unordered list.

A single data set on its own can already reveal useful information, but data becomes especially powerful once it is paired with a second, related data set collected about the same subjects, such as those same five students' hours spent studying alongside their matching quiz scores. Once two data sets are paired up this way, they can be plotted together on a coordinate plane to look for a relationship between them, which is exactly the idea explored in the very next chapter on scatterplots.
